walkthroughs.body_html:
A poverty trap is a self-reinforcing low-income equilibrium.

Low income → low saving → low investment → low capital → low income.

Other traps: malnutrition lowers productivity (Dasgupta), disease (Sachs), demographic (high fertility), institutional (weak property rights).

W.W. Rostow (1960): all economies pass through five stages.

1. Traditional society. 2. Pre-conditions for take-off. 3. Take-off. 4. Drive to maturity. 5. High mass consumption.

The 'take-off' requires investment > 10% of GDP, leading sectors and supportive institutions.

Critique: linear and Eurocentric; ignores colonial history.

W. Arthur Lewis (1954): an LDC has two sectors — traditional rural (subsistence) and modern industrial.

Surplus rural labour shifts to the modern sector at a constant wage. Capital accumulates and modern output expands.

The Lewis turning point arrives when surplus labour is exhausted and wages rise (cf. China c. 2010).

Ceteris paribus means everything happens at the same time in real markets.
'All other things equal' — when analysing the effect of one variable, all other variables are held constant. It is an analytical simplification, not a claim about reality.
Ceteris paribus is a Latin name for the equilibrium price.
